Intensification.q: A historian says the Silk Roads after 1200 were "not new, but busier." Which term names that idea?
wrong: Proto-industrialization, the expansion of Chinese iron, steel and porcelain output
That is about production, not the routes.
That is a community settled abroad.
Intensification.exp: Intensification: the same old routes carried more trade over longer distances.

Intensification.q: Which evidence would best support the claim that Silk Road trade intensified after 1200?
Intensification.right: More goods moving farther on the old routes
wrong: Brand-new roads being built across Central Asia for the first time in history
The routes were centuries old; that would be invention, not intensification.
Intensification.exp: Intensification means more trade over greater distances on routes that already existed.

Mongol stability.q: According to the textbook, what was the MOST significant cause of Silk Road growth after 1200?
Mongol stability.right: Mongol rule uniting and protecting the routes
wrong: The Crusades, which made Europeans want silk and spices from the East
A cause of demand, but not the textbook's main cause.
That was destruction, not a cause of growth.
Mongol stability.exp: The Mongols united the routes under one authority that protected merchants.

Mongol stability.q: Why would a merchant in 1280 feel safer crossing Central Asia than one in 1150?
Mongol stability.right: One authority punished bandits and kept roads up
wrong: Camels had just been brought to Central Asia from Arabia, making travel faster
Mongol stability.exp: Under the Mongols one authority enforced laws, improved roads and punished bandits.

Luxury goods demand.q: Why did artisans in China and Persia expand production for export after 1200?
wrong: Their own rulers banned them from selling any of their goods to local people
Not on your card; demand abroad drove it.
The routes were busier, not closed.
Luxury goods demand.exp: Elite demand for silk, porcelain, spices and fine textiles pushed artisans to produce for export.

Luxury goods demand.q: Which best explains why silk and porcelain, not grain, traveled the Silk Roads?
Luxury goods demand.right: Light, valuable goods for elite buyers
wrong: Grain could not grow anywhere along the Silk Roads, so it had to stay home
The reason is value and weight, not growing conditions.
Luxury goods demand.exp: The overland routes carried luxury goods that elites wanted.

Crusades (effect on demand).q: How did the Crusades affect trade between Europe and Asia?
Crusades (effect on demand).right: They raised European demand for Asian goods
wrong: They cut Europe off from Asian goods, since the crusaders closed the trade routes
Your card says they raised demand.
They had no effect on trade
Crusades (effect on demand).exp: Crusaders came home with eastern fabrics and spices, raising European demand.

Crusades (effect on demand).q: A European noble in 1250 wants silk he first saw on a relative who went east to fight. Which link does this show?
wrong: Mongol conquest → Chinese demand for European wool and other goods
The demand ran from Europe for Asian goods.
The plague came later and cut trade.
Crusades (effect on demand).exp: Returning crusaders spread a taste for Asian luxuries in Europe.

Caravan.q: Why did Silk Road merchants travel in caravans instead of alone?
wrong: Rulers required every merchant to pay a fee to join a group before leaving
Not on your card; the reason is safety.
Caravan.exp: A caravan of merchants, animals and guides was safer than traveling alone.

Caravan.q: Which pair of innovations both made caravan travel safer or cheaper?
wrong: Junks and lateen sails, which were used by traders all along the trade routes
Caravan.exp: Caravanserai gave shelter; better saddles raised loads.

Camel saddle (Silk Roads).q: What was the main effect of better camel saddles on Silk Road trade?
wrong: Camels could now drink less water, so they crossed the desert without stopping
Saddles changed loads, not water needs.
Camel saddle (Silk Roads).exp: Saddle design greatly increased the weight camels could carry.

Camel saddle (Silk Roads).q: Better saddles appear in both the Silk Road and trans-Saharan decks. What does that comparison show?
Camel saddle (Silk Roads).right: Both land networks depended on camels
wrong: Both networks were mainly sea routes that used camels to load and unload ships
Only the Silk Roads used camels
Camel saddle (Silk Roads).exp: Camel saddles raised loads on both overland networks.

Caravanserai.q: Why did caravanserai help trade grow?
wrong: They let merchants skip the long journey by sending goods through the mail
They were inns along the route.
Caravanserai.exp: Roadside inns with animal stalls, rooms and storage made travel safer and cheaper.

Caravanserai.q: Caravanserai, credit and paper money existed before 1200. How should you describe their role after 1200?
wrong: Invented for the very first time to serve the Mongols' new trade routes
Caravanserai.exp: Key point: improved and spread, not invented.

Money economy.q: Why did a money economy make long-distance trade easier than barter?
Money economy.right: Trade didn't depend on swapping goods
wrong: Money could be eaten if the trip ran short of food, unlike barter goods
Money is easier to move than goods.
Money economy.exp: With money, merchants didn't need someone who wanted their exact goods.

Money economy.q: Cowrie shells and salt appear on the money economy card. Why?
Money economy.right: They were goods used in barter
wrong: They were the first coins ever minted in China for long-distance trade
Money economy.exp: A money economy uses money instead of barter with goods like cowrie shells or salt.

Flying cash.q: Why did China develop flying cash?
Flying cash.right: Copper coins were too heavy for big trades
wrong: Merchants wanted to avoid paying taxes to the emperor on their goods
Not on your card; weight was the reason.
Flying cash.exp: Deposit in one place, withdraw elsewhere, because heavy coins were hard to carry.

Flying cash.q: Which European tool did the same job as China's flying cash?
wrong: The caravanserai, which stored goods so merchants didn't have to carry them
Flying cash.exp: Both let merchants move money without carrying coins.

Paper money.q: What problem did paper money solve?
wrong: Bandits could no longer rob caravans because paper was worthless to them
Paper money.exp: Paper money, first used in China, eased large transactions.

Paper money.q: Paper money was first used where?
wrong: Venice, where the first European banking houses opened in the 1300s
Banking houses came later in Europe.
Paper money.exp: Paper money was first used in China.

Bill of exchange.q: A Venetian merchant sells goods in Cairo and is promised a set payment on a set date. What document is this?
wrong: Flying cash, the Chinese system of depositing paper money in one place
Bill of exchange.exp: A bill of exchange promises a set payment on a set date.

Bill of exchange.q: Why would bills of exchange encourage merchants to travel farther?
wrong: Bills of exchange made it illegal for bandits to rob merchants on the road
They reduced risk by removing coins.
Bills were worth more than gold
Bill of exchange.exp: Merchants could move money without carrying coins.

Banking house.q: Where would a merchant with a bill of exchange go to have it cashed in the 1300s?
wrong: A caravanserai, the roadside inn where travelers kept their goods overnight
Banking house.exp: Banking houses handled bills and credit.

Banking house.q: Banking houses in Europe were a precursor to what?
wrong: Modern trading companies that hired their own armies to protect their trade
Banking house.exp: Banking houses were a precursor to modern banks.

Improved, not invented.q: A student writes, "Caravanserai were invented during the Mongol era." What's the correction?
Improved, not invented.right: They existed before 1200 and were improved
wrong: They were invented by the Ming dynasty after the Mongols had been overthrown
Your card says they existed before 1200.
Improved, not invented.exp: Caravanserai, credit and paper money existed before 1200; they were improved and spread.

Improved, not invented.q: Which describes CONTINUITY in commercial practices from before 1200 to after?
Improved, not invented.right: The same tools, used more and better
wrong: A complete break, with brand-new methods replacing the old ones everywhere
Improved, not invented.exp: The tools continued; their use was improved and spread.

Kashgar.q: Why did Kashgar become an important city?
Kashgar.right: Northern and southern routes met there
wrong: It was the capital of the Mongol Empire and home to Kublai Khan's court
Kashgar.exp: Kashgar was an oasis where Silk Road routes met.

Kashgar.q: Kashgar was once Buddhist and later a center of Islamic scholarship. What does this change show?
wrong: The Mongols forced everyone in their empire to convert to the same religion
Kashgar.exp: Religions spread along the trade routes that met at Kashgar.

Samarkand.q: What made Samarkand a "knot" of the Silk Roads?
Samarkand.right: It sat between China and the Mediterranean
wrong: It was a port on the Indian Ocean where monsoon ships unloaded their cargo
Samarkand.exp: Samarkand linked China and the Mediterranean.

Samarkand.q: Samarkand was religiously diverse and known for scholars. What does this suggest about trade cities?
Samarkand.right: They were also centers of ideas
wrong: They were closed to outsiders and only traded with people of one religion
Samarkand.exp: Trade cities like Samarkand drew people, faiths and learning.

wrong: The Mongols banned all farming, forcing peasants into factories in the cities
That came later and cut trade.
Proto-industrialization.exp: Demand pushed China to expand iron, steel and porcelain production.

Proto-industrialization.q: Which is an example of proto-industrialization?
Proto-industrialization.right: China expanding porcelain output for trade
wrong: Mongols building relay stations for messengers across the empire
Proto-industrialization.exp: Expanding iron, steel and porcelain production for trade.

Luxury production centers.q: Which regions expanded luxury production for export?
wrong: Mali, Russia and Japan, which made silk and porcelain for buyers in Europe
Your card names China, Persia and India.
Luxury production centers.exp: Chinese silk and porcelain and Persian and Indian textiles expanded for export.

Luxury production centers.q: How were luxury production centers and elite demand connected?
wrong: Production came first, and it later created demand once the goods appeared
Your cards say demand pushed production.
Luxury production centers.exp: Elite demand pushed artisans to expand production for export.

Temujin / Genghis Khan.q: Temujin promoted people for talent, not family ties. What did this help him do?
wrong: Win the support of Chinese scholars, who wanted the civil service exams kept
The Yuan later dismantled the exams.
Temujin / Genghis Khan.exp: He united the clans and promoted talent over family.

wrong: Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty and moved the capital to Dadu
The empire split into four khanates
Temujin / Genghis Khan.exp: The 1206 kuriltai elected Temujin, who became Genghis Khan.

Kuriltai.q: How did a new Mongol khan come to power, according to your cards?
Kuriltai.right: Chieftains elected him at a kuriltai
wrong: The oldest son always inherited the throne without any vote or meeting
Your card describes election by chiefs.
He was appointed by the caliph
Kuriltai.exp: A kuriltai was a meeting of chieftains; the 1206 one elected Temujin.

Kuriltai.q: Which modern idea is the kuriltai closest to?
Kuriltai.right: A council that chooses a leader
wrong: A court that tries criminals and decides what punishment they should get
Your card says it elected a khan.
Kuriltai.exp: The kuriltai was a meeting of chiefs that elected the khan.

Khan / khanate.q: The Golden Horde was ruled by a khan. What does that make the Golden Horde?
wrong: A caliphate, since it was ruled by the Mongols who later became Muslim
A caliphate is ruled by a caliph.
Khan / khanate.exp: A khanate is the kingdom of a khan.

wrong: Khan: the kingdom itself; khanate: the ruler who governs the kingdom
Khan: a merchant; khanate: a caravan
Khan: a priest; khanate: a temple
Khan / khanate.exp: A khan is a king; a khanate is his kingdom.

Mongol warfare.q: Which tactic involved pretending to run away to draw enemies into a trap?
wrong: Terrain mapping, studying the ground before an attack to plan the battle
That's mapping, not a fake retreat.
Mongol warfare.exp: Feigned retreats were part of Mongol warfare.

Mongol warfare.q: Why could the Mongols take walled cities, though they were steppe horsemen?
wrong: They had always built stone cities of their own and knew how walls worked
They were nomads; they borrowed the know-how.
The cities surrendered without fighting every time
Mongol warfare.exp: The Mongols adopted conquered peoples' technology.

Siege weapons.q: Where did the Mongols get the skills to build catapults and siege towers?
wrong: Their own nomadic tradition of building wooden machines on the steppe
Siege weapons.exp: Siege weapons were built with captured Chinese and Persian engineers.

Siege weapons.q: What does the Mongols' use of siege weapons show about their empire?
wrong: They refused to use any ideas that came from outside the Mongol clans
Siege weapons.exp: Skilled captives helped the Mongols take walled cities.

Mongol motive.q: Why did the Mongols recruit miners, scribes and craftworkers from conquered lands?
wrong: They wanted to convert them to the Mongol religion before sending them home

Mongol motive.q: What drew the Mongols toward lands near the Silk Roads?
Mongol motive.right: The wealth there, like silk and gold
wrong: The religious sites they wanted to protect from attacks by crusaders
Those lands were rich and populated.
Mongol motive.exp: The Mongols coveted the wealth of their neighbors.

Yuan Dynasty.q: How was the Yuan different from the Mongols' homeland style of rule?
Yuan Dynasty.right: It was more Chinese in style
wrong: It was the most traditionally Mongol of all the khanates in the empire
Yuan Dynasty.exp: The Yuan was more Chinese in style and rebuilt the capital as Dadu.

Yuan Dynasty.q: Which dynasty replaced the Yuan in 1368?
wrong: The Song, which had ruled China before the Mongols arrived in the 1200s
The Song came before the Yuan.
Yuan Dynasty.exp: The Yuan (1271–1368) was ended by the Ming.

Il-khanate.q: Who ran the day-to-day government in the Il-khanate?
wrong: Mongol warriors, who refused to let any conquered people work in government
Il-khanate.exp: Persians served as officials in the Il-khanate.

Il-khanate.q: The Mongols of the Il-khanate later converted to Islam. Which broader pattern does this show?
wrong: Mongols forcing their own religion on the people they had conquered
The Mongols took on local faiths.
Il-khanate.exp: Assimilation into local cultures is one cause of Mongol decline.

wrong: The Yuan dynasty, which ruled China until it was overthrown in the 1300s
Your card says the Golden Horde lasted longest.

Golden Horde.q: How did the Golden Horde control Russia?
Golden Horde.right: Through Russian princes who paid tribute
wrong: By replacing all Russian leaders with Mongol governors from the steppe
Golden Horde.exp: The Golden Horde ruled through Russian princes who paid tribute.

Chagatai Khanate.q: Which khanate kept the most traditional Mongol ways?
wrong: The Yuan dynasty, which kept Mongol customs in its capital at Dadu
The Yuan was more Chinese in style.
It used Persians and converted to Islam.
Chagatai Khanate.exp: The Chagatai Khanate in Central Asia stayed the most traditionally Mongol.

Chagatai Khanate.q: Compare the Yuan and the Chagatai Khanate.
Chagatai Khanate.right: The Yuan adapted; the Chagatai stayed Mongol
wrong: Both took on local customs and converted to Islam in the same way
The Yuan became Chinese-style; Chagatai stayed traditional.
Chagatai Khanate.exp: The Yuan was more Chinese in style; the Chagatai stayed the most traditionally Mongol.

Kublai Khan.q: Marco Polo was welcomed at Kublai Khan's court. What does that show about Kublai?
wrong: He banned outsiders from China to protect it from European ideas
Kublai Khan.exp: Kublai welcomed foreigners such as Marco Polo.

Kublai Khan.q: How was Kublai related to Hulegu?
wrong: Kublai was Hulegu's father, who sent him west to conquer Persia
They were enemies from different clans
Kublai Khan.exp: Your cards call both Genghis Khan's grandsons.

Hulegu.q: Why was Hulegu's capture of Baghdad in 1258 a turning point?
Hulegu.right: He destroyed the city and killed the caliph
wrong: He made Baghdad the new capital of the Yuan dynasty and moved there
Hulegu.exp: Hulegu destroyed Baghdad and killed the caliph.

wrong: The Golden Horde, which conquered Russia and destroyed Kiev in 1240
Hulegu.exp: Hulegu founded the Il-khanate in Persia.

Indirect rule.q: What was an advantage of the Golden Horde's indirect rule?
wrong: It let the Mongols replace the Russian language with their own across the land
Indirect rule.exp: Existing Russian princes ruled and sent tribute.

Indirect rule.q: Which other example uses local elites to govern, like the Golden Horde did?
wrong: The Yuan hiring foreigners and keeping the Chinese out of government
Indirect rule.exp: Both relied on local people to govern.

Pax Mongolica.q: Why did the Pax Mongolica boost trade?
wrong: It ended all trade between Europe and China to protect Mongol merchants
Pax Mongolica.exp: Safer routes, maintained roads, punished banditry and tolerance boosted trade.

Pax Mongolica.q: Which is a COST of the same Mongol connections that made the Pax Mongolica possible?
wrong: Ending Silk Road trade by closing every road through Mongol territory
Pax Mongolica.exp: Your cards say Mongol conquests helped transmit the plague.

Yam.q: What was the purpose of the yam?
wrong: Carrying trade goods from China to Europe for the Mongol khans
Yam.exp: The yam was a relay messenger system.

Yam.q: How did the yam help the Mongols hold a huge empire?
wrong: It let the Mongols move the capital to a new city every single year
Yam.exp: The relay system linked the far reaches of the empire.

Religious tolerance.q: Why was Mongol religious tolerance good for trade?
Religious tolerance.right: Merchants of every faith could trade
wrong: It forced every merchant to adopt the same religion as the khan
Your card says it was unusual.
Religious tolerance.exp: Allowing many religions was unusual and helpful to trade.

Religious tolerance.q: How was Mongol tolerance unusual for the 13th century?
wrong: They allowed only one official religion and punished anyone who refused it
Religious tolerance.exp: Genghis and Kublai allowed many religions.

Greco-Islamic medical knowledge.q: How did Greek medicine reach Western Europe?
Greco-Islamic medical knowledge.right: Through Islamic scholars and Mongol-era contact
wrong: Directly from Greece, without passing through any other cultures on the way
Your card traces it through Islamic scholars.
Greco-Islamic medical knowledge.exp: Greek medicine, advanced by scholars like Ibn Sina, reached Europe via Mongol-era contact.

Greco-Islamic medical knowledge.q: Which scholar advanced Greek medicine in the Islamic world?
wrong: Ibn Battuta, the Moroccan scholar who traveled through Mali and China

Numbering systems.q: Where did the numbers Europeans call "Arabic" begin?
wrong: Arabia, which is why Europeans named the numbers after the Arabs

Numbering systems.q: Hindu-Arabic numerals reaching Europe is an example of what?
Numbering systems.right: Transfer of ideas along trade networks
wrong: Transfer of crops from one region to another along the trade routes
Numbering systems.exp: Ideas moved with trade during the Mongol era.

Uyghur script.q: Why did the Mongols adopt the Uyghur script?
Uyghur script.right: To write Mongol and run the empire
wrong: To replace Chinese writing everywhere in the Yuan dynasty with Uyghur
Uyghur script.exp: The Uyghur script was adapted for the Mongol language to help run the empire.

Uyghur script.q: The Uyghur script and siege weapons have what in common?
wrong: Both were invented by Genghis Khan himself to help him rule the clans
Uyghur script.exp: The Mongols adopted tools from others.

Causes of Mongol decline.q: Which cause of Mongol decline came from INSIDE the ruling family?
wrong: The Black Death, which killed many people along the empire's trade routes

Causes of Mongol decline.q: How did the empire's vast size contribute to decline?
Causes of Mongol decline.right: It was hard to hold together
wrong: It gave the Mongols too much trade, which made them stop fighting entirely
Causes of Mongol decline.exp: Vast distances, along with other causes, weakened the empire.

Foreign officials (Yuan grievance).q: Why did Chinese scholar-gentry resent the Yuan?
Foreign officials (Yuan grievance).right: Foreigners took jobs; exams were dismantled
wrong: The Yuan forced every scholar to move to Mongolia and learn to ride horses
The Yuan raised them to power
Foreign officials (Yuan grievance).exp: Yuan rulers hired foreigners and dismantled the civil service exams.

Foreign officials (Yuan grievance).q: Compare Yuan rule with the Il-khanate's.
Foreign officials (Yuan grievance).right: The Il-khanate used locals; the Yuan didn't
wrong: Both hired local people for government and both kept the old civil service
The Yuan shut the Chinese out.
Foreign officials (Yuan grievance).exp: Persians served as Il-khanate officials; the Yuan hired foreigners instead of Chinese.

White Lotus Society.q: What role did the White Lotus Society play in the 1350s?
wrong: It supported the Yuan by collecting taxes from Chinese peasants for the khan
White Lotus Society.exp: A secret society organizing against the Yuan.

White Lotus Society.q: Which event did the White Lotus Society help lead to?
White Lotus Society.right: The fall of the Yuan and rise of the Ming
wrong: The founding of the Yuan dynasty under Kublai Khan in 1271
White Lotus Society.exp: Organized resistance helped end the Yuan in 1368.

Zhu Yuanzhang.q: What was unusual about the man who founded the Ming?
Zhu Yuanzhang.right: He was a poor peasant's son and a monk
wrong: He was a Mongol prince who switched sides and joined the Chinese rebels
Zhu Yuanzhang.exp: Zhu Yuanzhang was a Buddhist monk from a poor peasant family.

Zhu Yuanzhang.q: Which card shows the result of the Yuan's grievances?
wrong: Kublai Khan welcoming Marco Polo and other foreigners to his court
Zhu Yuanzhang.exp: Resentment and revolt led to Zhu Yuanzhang overthrowing the Yuan in 1368.

Tamerlane (Timur).q: Which city did Tamerlane ravage in 1389–90?
wrong: Baghdad, which the Mongols under Hulegu had already destroyed in 1258

Tamerlane (Timur).q: Tamerlane taking Central Asia around 1369 fits which larger story?
Tamerlane (Timur).right: New powers filling the Mongol gap
wrong: The Mongol Empire reaching its greatest size under a single Great Khan
Tamerlane (Timur).exp: As the Mongols declined, conquerors like Tamerlane took their lands.

Mongol legacy.q: Why does your card call the Mongols "destroyers AND connectors"?
Mongol legacy.right: They wrecked cities but linked trade
wrong: They destroyed every trade route they found and connected nothing at all
Mongol legacy.exp: The Mongols were both destructive and connecting.

Mongol legacy.q: What is one lasting idea the Mongols spread?
wrong: Democracy, with leaders chosen by every person in the empire through voting
Not their legacy on your card.
Mongol legacy.exp: They spread ideas of centralized government.

Monsoon winds.q: Why did Indian Ocean merchants often wait in port for months?
Monsoon winds.right: For the winds to reverse direction
wrong: For the Ming emperor to give them permission to sail to the next port
Your card says the seasonal winds.
For their ships to be rebuilt
Monsoon winds.exp: Merchants timed voyages to the monsoon and waited for it to reverse.

Monsoon winds.q: A ship leaves India for East Africa. In which season would winds from the northeast carry it?
wrong: Summer, when the monsoon blows from the southwest across the ocean
Summer winds blow from the southwest.
Winter winds come from the northeast.
Monsoon winds.exp: Winter monsoon winds come from the northeast.

Lateen sail.q: What advantage did the lateen sail give sailors?
Lateen sail.right: It caught wind from many directions
wrong: It let ships sail without any wind at all by using the force of ocean currents
Lateen sail.exp: The triangular lateen sail catches wind from many directions.

Lateen sail.q: Your card says the lateen sail's origin is debated. How should you write about it?
Lateen sail.right: Say Arab sailors used it; don't claim who invented it
wrong: Say it was a Chinese invention, the same as the compass and the stern rudder
Lateen sail.exp: It was used by Arab sailors; its origin is debated.

Stern rudder.q: Which problem did the stern rudder solve?
wrong: Finding a ship's latitude by measuring the angle of the stars at night
Stern rudder.exp: The stern rudder improved stability and steering.

Stern rudder.q: The stern rudder and magnetic compass share which origin?
wrong: Both were improved by Muslim navigators in the twelfth century for Arab ships

Magnetic compass.q: How did the magnetic compass spread from China?
wrong: Through the Mongol yam, which carried it overland from China to Europe
Your card says through sea trade.
Magnetic compass.exp: The compass spread across the seas through trade.

Magnetic compass.q: Which tool let sailors keep a heading even when clouds hid the stars?
wrong: The astrolabe, which measured how far north or south the ship had traveled
Magnetic compass.exp: A compass points the way without needing the sky.

Astrolabe.q: What did an astrolabe tell a sailor?
Astrolabe.right: How far north or south of the equator the ship was
wrong: How fast the ship was moving through the water compared to the wind
Astrolabe.exp: The astrolabe shows how far north or south of the equator a ship is.

Astrolabe.q: Who improved the astrolabe in the 12th century?
wrong: Chinese admirals such as Zheng He, who led the Ming treasure fleets

Dhow.q: Compare a dhow and a junk.
Dhow.right: Dhow: small Arab/Indian; junk: large Chinese
wrong: Dhow: a large Chinese ship; junk: a small Arab ship with lateen sails
Dhow.exp: Dhows were small Arab and Indian ships; junks were large Chinese ships.

wrong: Square sails of woven silk, which the Chinese supplied to Arab merchants

Junk.q: What feature made Chinese junks able to carry huge cargoes?
Junk.right: Large size with a compartmented hull
wrong: A single small triangular sail that could catch the wind from any direction
That's a lateen sail; junks had several sails.
Oars rowed by hundreds of slaves
Junk.exp: Junks had multiple sails, compartmented hulls and could be up to 400 feet long.

Junk.q: Which fleet would most likely have been made of junks?
wrong: The Swahili traders' fleets sailing between Kilwa and Mombasa
Junk.exp: Junks were Chinese ships, like those of the Ming fleets.

Specialized products.q: Which region was known for gold and ivory?
wrong: Southwest Asia, which sent horses and dates to other ports on the ocean
Specialized products.exp: Gold, ivory and slaves came from the Swahili coast.

Specialized products.q: Why did regional specialties make the Indian Ocean network grow?
Specialized products.right: Each region had goods others wanted
wrong: Every region produced the same goods, so merchants traded only for money
The point is that regions differed.
Specialized products.exp: Different specialties gave every region something to trade.

Calicut.q: Why was Calicut called the "City of Spices"?
Calicut.right: It was a major spice port
wrong: It was the only place in the world where pepper and spices could grow
Your card says it was a port known for spices.
Calicut.exp: Calicut was a southwest Indian port known for spices.

Calicut.q: Why did Arab and Chinese merchants both come to Calicut?
wrong: The Mongols forced merchants to trade there instead of at other ports
It was the capital of Mali
Gold mines that supplied the trans-Saharan caravans with gold for salt

Gujarat.q: Gujarat and Malacca both grew rich in what way?
wrong: Selling gold that they mined themselves to merchants from the north
Gujarat.exp: Both collected customs and fees from passing trade.

Swahili city-states.q: What does the Swahili language show about East Africa's coast?
Swahili city-states.right: Blending of Bantu and Arabic cultures
wrong: That East Africans refused contact with any outside traders or cultures
Swahili city-states.exp: The Swahili language blends Bantu and Arabic, a result of trade contact.

Swahili city-states.q: What did Swahili city-states trade for Chinese porcelain and Indian cotton?
wrong: Silk and tea, which they made themselves for sale to merchants from China
Swahili city-states.exp: Swahili cities exchanged gold and ivory for porcelain and cotton.

Sultanate of Malacca.q: Why could Malacca grow rich without producing much itself?
Sultanate of Malacca.right: It charged ships passing the strait
wrong: It mined gold and sold it to Chinese merchants, who carried it home
Your card says fees on ships.
Sultanate of Malacca.exp: Malacca grew rich from fees on ships passing the Strait of Malacca.

Sultanate of Malacca.q: Why did Malacca build a navy?
Sultanate of Malacca.right: To control the strait and its fees
wrong: To conquer China and replace the Ming as the strongest power in Asia
To fight the Mongols in Russia
Sultanate of Malacca.exp: A navy let Malacca control shipping through the strait (an example of centralization).

Customs duties.q: How did states benefit from Indian Ocean trade without trading themselves?
wrong: By forcing merchants to give them their ships at the end of every voyage
Customs duties.exp: Taxes on imports and port fees gave states revenue.

Customs duties.q: Which card is the clearest example of customs duties?
wrong: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage, which displayed Mali's wealth to the world

Diaspora.q: Arab merchants settled in Calicut and kept their customs while adopting some local ones. What is this?
wrong: A caravanserai, a place where merchants stayed while trading in a city
Diaspora.exp: A diaspora is a community settled away from home that shares traditions both ways.

Diaspora.q: How does a diaspora change BOTH the settlers and the locals?
wrong: The settlers completely replace the local culture with their own culture
Diaspora.exp: Settlers introduce traditions and are influenced in turn.

Merchant intermarriage.q: How did Islam spread in many Indian Ocean ports?
wrong: Through armies that conquered each port and forced people to convert
Your card says family ties, not conquest.
Merchant intermarriage.exp: Arab and Persian merchants married locally, spreading Islam through family ties.

Merchant intermarriage.q: Compare how Islam spread in Indian Ocean ports and in West Africa.
wrong: Both spread mainly through military conquest by Arab and Persian armies
Merchant intermarriage.exp: Indian Ocean: intermarriage. West Africa: merchants and rulers' conversions, not conquest.

Zheng He.q: What were Zheng He's voyages meant to do?
Zheng He.right: Show Ming power and collect tribute
wrong: Conquer East Africa and set up Chinese colonies along the Swahili coast
Zheng He.exp: To show Ming power, collect tribute and open markets.

Zheng He.q: How far did Zheng He's fleets reach?
wrong: Only to Japan and Korea, since Ming ships couldn't cross the open ocean
Zheng He.exp: Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa.

End of the voyages.q: Why did China stop Zheng He's voyages?
End of the voyages.right: Cost and Confucian fear of foreign contact
wrong: Zheng He's fleets were destroyed by the Portuguese navy in the Indian Ocean
End of the voyages.exp: Confucian scholars feared foreign contact and the cost.

End of the voyages.q: What was a result of ending the voyages?
wrong: China built an even bigger fleet to send to Africa and the Middle East
End of the voyages.exp: Yongle's successor ended the voyages and discouraged sailing abroad.

Indian Ocean slave trade.q: How did the Indian Ocean slave trade differ from the later Atlantic one?
Indian Ocean slave trade.right: Mostly urban, household and military work
wrong: It sent enslaved people mainly to sugar plantations in the Americas
To North Africa, the Middle East and India.
Indian Ocean slave trade.exp: Enslaved East Africans often did urban labor, household work or soldiering.

Indian Ocean slave trade.q: Where were enslaved East Africans sold in this period?
Indian Ocean slave trade.right: North Africa, the Middle East and India
wrong: The Americas, where they worked on sugar plantations owned by Europeans
Indian Ocean slave trade.exp: To North Africa, the Middle East and India.

Sahara and oases.q: Why did trans-Saharan caravans travel from oasis to oasis?
wrong: Rulers required merchants to pay taxes at every oasis they came to
Sahara and oases.exp: In the huge arid Sahara, only small oases had water.

Sahara and oases.q: How big was the Sahara, according to your card?
wrong: About the size of a single city like Timbuktu, so it was easy to cross
Your card compares it to China.
Sahara and oases.exp: The Sahara is about the size of China.

Camel.q: Why did camels replace horses and donkeys in North Africa?
Camel.right: They could go long without water
wrong: They were faster than horses over short distances on grass and roads
They were cheaper to feed meat
Camel.exp: Camels drink over 50 gallons quickly and travel long without water.

Camel.q: When did camels replace horses and donkeys in North Africa?
wrong: After 1200 CE, when the Mongols united the trade routes across Asia

Camel saddle.q: What made heavy camel freight practical across the Sahara?
Camel saddle.right: Somali saddles carrying up to 600 pounds
wrong: Wheeled carts that camels pulled across the sand from oasis to oasis
Camel saddle.exp: A saddle developed by the Somalis carried loads of up to 600 pounds.

Camel saddle.q: Who developed the camel saddle on the trans-Saharan card?
wrong: The Chinese, who also invented the compass and the stern rudder

Trans-Saharan caravan.q: Which helped merchants trust each other across distant cities?
wrong: Mongol law codes enforced by the khan's officials in every oasis town
Trans-Saharan caravan.exp: Family partners, credit and agents linked cities.

Trans-Saharan caravan.q: Compare trans-Saharan caravans with Silk Road caravans.
Trans-Saharan caravan.right: Both traveled in large groups for safety
wrong: Trans-Saharan caravans used ships while the Silk Road caravans used camels
Silk Road caravans had no animals
Trans-Saharan caravan.exp: Both moved in organized groups with guides and animals.

Gold.q: Why did foreign traders come to West Africa?
wrong: Its silk and porcelain, which were the finest available anywhere
Gold.exp: Gold was the most precious trans-Saharan good and drew foreign traders.

wrong: South, from North Africa to the trading cities of West Africa
Salt went south; gold went north.
Gold.exp: Gold went north from West Africa.

Salt.q: Why was salt traded south for gold?
wrong: It was mined in West Africa and sent north to oasis towns such as Taghaza
It was used as paper money
Salt.exp: Salt came from North Africa, such as the Taghaza oasis.

Salt.q: Which pair names the core trans-Saharan exchange?
wrong: Silk for horses, which were traded between Chinese and Central Asian merchants
Salt.exp: Gold went north; salt went south.

Trans-Saharan goods.q: Which good moved from north to south?
wrong: Kola nuts, which were grown in the forests of West Africa for sale
Trans-Saharan goods.exp: North to south: salt, textiles, horses, copper and brass.

Trans-Saharan goods.q: Which good moved from south to north?
wrong: Copper and brass, which were made in the north and sold in West Africa
Trans-Saharan goods.exp: South to north: gold, ivory, slaves, kola nuts.

Cowrie shells.q: What were cowrie shells used for in West African cities?
wrong: As decoration for mosques and schools built by Mansa Musa in Timbuktu
Cowrie shells.exp: Cowrie shells were used as currency.

Cowrie shells.q: Cowrie shells and Chinese flying cash appear on the same card. Which?
wrong: Indian Ocean profile, which lists the goods carried on dhows and junks
That card lists ships and tools.
Cowrie shells.exp: The Currencies card lists silk and tin ingots, cowrie shells, coins and flying cash.

Mali Empire.q: How did Mali become richer than Ghana?
wrong: It conquered China and took control of the Silk Roads' silk trade

Mali Empire.q: Mali and the Mongols both grew rich partly by doing what?
wrong: Banning merchants from crossing their land without first converting
Neither is known for that here.
Mali Empire.exp: Stable states that protected trade grew rich (see the Stable states card).

wrong: Mansa Musa, the ruler famous for his lavish pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324

Sundiata.right: Returned from exile and defeated his rivals
wrong: Made a lavish pilgrimage to Mecca that displayed Mali's wealth to the world
Sundiata.exp: Sundiata returned from exile in 1235 and defeated his rivals.

Mansa Musa.q: What did Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage show the world?
wrong: Mali's military power, which it used to conquer Mecca on the journey
Mansa Musa.exp: His lavish pilgrimage displayed Mali's wealth.

Mansa Musa.q: What did Mansa Musa do after his pilgrimage?
Mansa Musa.right: Built mosques and schools in Timbuktu
wrong: Moved Mali's capital to Mecca so he could be closer to the holy city
Mansa Musa.exp: He built mosques and schools in Timbuktu.

wrong: Building the largest ships in Africa for trade across the Indian Ocean
Timbuktu.exp: Timbuktu became a world-renowned center of Islamic learning.

Timbuktu.q: Timbuktu and Samarkand were both what?
Timbuktu.right: Trade cities that became centers of learning
wrong: Ports on the Indian Ocean where monsoon ships unloaded their goods
Both are tied to Islamic learning.
Timbuktu.exp: Both were trade "knots" and centers of learning.

wrong: Ghana, which Mali had already surpassed in wealth during the 1200s
Songhai.exp: Songhai replaced Mali in the late 1400s.

Songhai.q: In what order did these West African powers rise?
wrong: Songhai, Mali and then Ghana, which became the richest of the three
Songhai.exp: Mali became richer than Ghana; Songhai replaced Mali.

Spread of Islam in West Africa.q: How did Islam spread in West Africa?
wrong: Through conquest by Arab armies that forced everyone in the region to convert
Spread of Islam in West Africa.exp: Merchants and rulers' conversions, not conquest.

Spread of Islam in West Africa.q: What does "most West Africans kept traditional beliefs" suggest?
Spread of Islam in West Africa.right: Islam spread mainly among rulers and merchants
wrong: Islam was banned in West Africa and only practiced in secret by traders
Spread of Islam in West Africa.exp: Islam spread through merchants and rulers, while most people kept traditional beliefs.

Buddhism in East Asia.q: Which path did Buddhism follow into East Asia?
wrong: China → India → Persia, carried west by Mongol armies after 1200
It started in India and moved east.
Buddhism in East Asia.exp: Buddhism came from India along the Silk Roads, then reached Korea and Japan.

Buddhism in East Asia.q: What role did the monk Xuanzang play?
Buddhism in East Asia.right: He helped popularize Buddhism in China
wrong: He founded the Ming dynasty after leading a peasant revolt against the Yuan
Buddhism in East Asia.exp: Xuanzang helped popularize Buddhism in China.

Chan (Zen) Buddhism.q: Chan Buddhism blends Buddhism with which tradition?
wrong: Islam, which reached China along the same Silk Road routes as Buddhism
Chan (Zen) Buddhism.exp: Chan (Zen) blends Buddhism with Daoist ideas.

Chan (Zen) Buddhism.q: Chan Buddhism is an example of which process?
wrong: Diaspora, a community of settlers living away from their original homeland
Chan (Zen) Buddhism.exp: Blending religions into a new faith is syncretism.

Neo-Confucianism.q: Which country made Neo-Confucianism its state ideology?
wrong: Mali, which adopted it after merchants brought it across the Sahara
Neo-Confucianism.exp: Korea made Neo-Confucianism its state ideology.

wrong: Both were brought to China from Europe by merchants such as Marco Polo
Neo-Confucianism.exp: Both are syncretic: Chan mixes Buddhism and Daoism; Neo-Confucianism mixes Confucian, Daoist and Buddhist ideas.

Syncretism.q: Which is an example of syncretism?
Syncretism.right: Chan Buddhism blending Buddhism with Daoism
wrong: Mongols destroying Baghdad and killing the caliph in the year 1258
Syncretism.exp: Chan Buddhism blends Buddhism with Daoist ideas: syncretism.

Syncretism.q: How does syncretism differ from conversion?
Syncretism.right: It blends faiths instead of replacing one
wrong: It forces people to give up their old religion and accept a new one
Syncretism.exp: Syncretism blends beliefs into a new faith.

wrong: That Islam was the main religion of the Khmer Empire in this period
Your card says Hindu and Buddhist.
Hinduism and Buddhism in Southeast Asia.exp: The Khmer Empire's Angkor monuments show both Hindu and Buddhist influences.

Hinduism and Buddhism in Southeast Asia.q: How did Hinduism and Buddhism reach Southeast Asia?
wrong: Through conquest by Mongol armies sent south by Kublai Khan from China

Islam in Africa and Asia.q: Which ways did Islam spread, according to this card?
wrong: Only through the Mongols, who forced every conquered people to convert
That's one way in the Indian Ocean.
Islam in Africa and Asia.exp: Islam spread by merchants, missionaries and conquest.

Islam in Africa and Asia.q: Which is an effect of Islam's spread named on your card?
wrong: The founding of the Yuan dynasty in China by Kublai Khan in 1271
Islam in Africa and Asia.exp: Islam shaped Swahili culture, Timbuktu's learning and South Asian architecture and language.

Urdu.q: Urdu blends Hindi with which influences?
wrong: Chinese and Mongol, from the Yuan officials who governed northern India
Urdu.exp: Urdu blends Hindi with Arabic and Persian.

Urdu.q: Urdu and Swahili are both examples of what?
wrong: Languages invented by rulers to keep their governments secret
Urdu.exp: Urdu (Hindi + Persian + Arabic) and Swahili (Bantu + Arabic) came from contact.

Gunpowder.q: How did gunpowder change the world after it spread west?
wrong: It changed farming, since it was used to clear forests for new crops
Gunpowder.exp: Gunpowder spread west and changed warfare.

Gunpowder.q: Gunpowder and papermaking share which origin?
wrong: Both were invented by Islamic scholars and carried to China by merchants
Gunpowder.exp: Both are Chinese inventions that spread west.

Papermaking.q: How did papermaking change Europe after the 13th century?
Papermaking.right: Books got cheaper and literacy rose
wrong: Paper money replaced all coins in Europe within a few years of its arrival
Papermaking.exp: Paper made books cheaper and raised literacy and record-keeping.

wrong: The 8th century, when Arab merchants revived the old Silk Road routes
Papermaking.exp: Papermaking reached Europe in the 13th century.

Islamic scholars as translators.q: Why do historians say Islamic scholars "saved the Greeks"?
Islamic scholars as translators.right: They translated Greek classics into Arabic
wrong: They protected Greece from Mongol invasion by sending armies to defend it
Islamic scholars as translators.exp: They translated works by Aristotle and others into Arabic.

Islamic scholars as translators.q: What did Islamic scholars add besides Greek works?
wrong: Silk-making and porcelain techniques that they brought from China
Islamic scholars as translators.exp: They added mathematics from India and advances in medicine.

Hangzhou.right: Size and its place on the Grand Canal
wrong: It was the capital of the Mongol Empire and home of the kuriltai
Hangzhou.exp: Hangzhou had about a million people at the southern end of the Grand Canal.

Hangzhou.q: Hangzhou had a thriving Arab community. What does this show?
Hangzhou.right: Foreign merchants settled in Chinese cities
wrong: China banned all foreigners from entering its cities during this time
Hangzhou.exp: An Arab community shows a merchant diaspora in China.

Why cities grew.q: Which factor would MOST help a city grow?
wrong: Invasion by a foreign army that destroys the walls and markets of the city
Why cities grew.exp: Stability, safe transport, commerce, labor and farm output helped cities grow.

Why cities grew.q: More farm output helped cities grow. Why?
wrong: It made people leave the cities to go back and work on the farms
Why cities grew.exp: Plentiful food supports larger city populations.

Why cities declined.q: Which card shows a city declining for reasons on the "Why cities declined" card?
wrong: Hangzhou, which grew to about a million people on the Grand Canal
Why cities declined.exp: Constantinople was weakened by crusade, plague and invasion.

Why cities declined.q: Which pair of causes of decline are opposites of causes of growth?
Why cities declined.right: Instability vs. stability; falling vs. more farm output
wrong: Safe transport vs. commerce, since both of them helped the city to grow
Why cities declined.exp: Stability and farm output build cities; instability and falling output weaken them.

wrong: The Mongol conquest of the city and the founding of the Golden Horde there
Constantinople.exp: The Fourth Crusade (1204) and plague (1346 and 1349) weakened it.

wrong: The Mongols of the Golden Horde, who had already conquered Kiev in 1240
Constantinople.exp: Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453.

Marco Polo.q: What did Marco Polo's account focus on?
wrong: Religious pilgrimages to Jerusalem, Rome and Spain made by Christians
Marco Polo.exp: Marco Polo focused on trade and cities.

Marco Polo.q: Why would a historian check Marco Polo against other sources?
Marco Polo.right: Many Europeans doubted him; his view was a merchant's
wrong: He wrote in Chinese, so Europeans could never read what he had written
Marco Polo.exp: His point of view was a merchant's, and many Europeans doubted him.

Ibn Battuta.q: Why did Ibn Battuta mostly visit Muslim lands?
wrong: He was a Venetian merchant looking for spices and silk to sell at home
Non-Muslim lands were closed to all travelers
Ibn Battuta.exp: A Moroccan Muslim scholar who visited mostly Muslim lands.

Ibn Battuta.q: Compare Ibn Battuta and Marco Polo as sources.
Ibn Battuta.right: A scholar's eye vs. a merchant's eye
wrong: Both wrote from a Christian point of view about pilgrimages to holy sites
Ibn Battuta.exp: Ibn Battuta wrote as a Muslim scholar; Polo as a merchant.

Margery Kempe.q: What does Margery Kempe's book offer that Polo's and Ibn Battuta's don't?
wrong: A description of China written by someone who served in Kublai's court
Margery Kempe.exp: Kempe shows a middle-class woman's life and Christian pilgrimages.

Margery Kempe.q: Where did Margery Kempe make pilgrimages?
wrong: Mecca, Cairo and Timbuktu, following the route Mansa Musa had taken

Reading travel accounts.q: Before using a travel account as evidence, what should you note first?
wrong: Whether the writer used paper or parchment, since that proves it is genuine
Reading travel accounts.exp: Travel accounts are shaped by the writer's religion, culture and purpose.

Reading travel accounts.q: Ibn Battuta criticizes customs in a non-Muslim town. How should you read that?
Reading travel accounts.right: As shaped by his Muslim point of view
wrong: As a completely neutral report, since travelers always describe things fairly
Accounts are shaped by the writer.
Point of view doesn't make it false.
Reading travel accounts.exp: Always note the writer's religion, culture and purpose.

Champa rice.q: Why did Champa rice lead to population growth in China?
Champa rice.right: Two crops a year, even in drought or flood
wrong: It was a luxury good that elites bought at high prices from Champa
It was a staple that fed people.
Champa rice.exp: Quick-ripening, drought- and flood-resistant rice yielded two crops a year.

Champa rice.q: How did Champa rice reach China?
wrong: Through the trans-Saharan caravans that carried goods from West Africa
Champa rice.exp: It came from Champa and was offered to China as tribute.

Bananas.q: How did bananas change Sub-Saharan Africa?
Bananas.right: Population grew; Bantu-speakers settled new areas
wrong: Bananas replaced gold as the main good traded north across the Sahara
Bananas.exp: Bananas boosted population and let Bantu speakers settle where yams didn't grow.

Bananas.q: Who brought bananas to Sub-Saharan Africa?
wrong: Chinese admirals on Zheng He's voyages, who also brought porcelain

Citrus crops.q: How did citrus crops reach the Mediterranean?
wrong: Through Chinese junks that sailed directly from China to the Mediterranean
Citrus crops.exp: Citrus spread through Muslim lands and markets such as Samarkand.

Citrus crops.q: Champa rice, bananas and citrus all show what?
wrong: Crops never moved between regions before the Europeans arrived
Citrus crops.exp: Crops moved along trade networks and changed diets and populations.

Sugar and cotton.q: How did sugar and cotton first spread, according to your card?
wrong: Through Mongol rule, which planted them along the roads of Central Asia

Sugar and cotton.q: What later effect of sugar does your card warn about?
wrong: Sugar caused the Black Death by attracting rats into the trading ports
Sugar and cotton.exp: Later European demand for sugar fueled mass use of enslaved labor in the Americas.

Environmental degradation.q: Why did growing populations lead to environmental degradation?
wrong: More people planted forests, which blocked sunlight from reaching the crops
Environmental degradation.exp: Larger populations caused overgrazing, deforestation and soil erosion.

Environmental degradation.q: Which result of environmental degradation is on your card?
wrong: Trade grew much faster because there was more land available for farming
Environmental degradation.exp: Overgrazing, deforestation and erosion cut farm output.

Overgrazing and soil erosion.q: Why was Great Zimbabwe abandoned in the late 1400s?
wrong: The Mongols invaded and destroyed the city's walls with siege weapons
Overgrazing and soil erosion.exp: Overgrazing near Great Zimbabwe forced people to abandon the city.

Overgrazing and soil erosion.q: Which region does your card say was hurt by deforestation and soil erosion?
wrong: Ming China, which cut down forests to build Zheng He's huge ships
Overgrazing and soil erosion.exp: Deforestation and soil erosion hurt feudal Europe.

Bubonic plague (Black Death).q: How did the Black Death reach Europe?
Bubonic plague (Black Death).right: Along trade routes from Central Asia
wrong: From the Americas, carried back by European ships after the voyages
Not on your card; it came from Central Asia.
Bubonic plague (Black Death).exp: The plague spread along trade routes from Central Asia.

Bubonic plague (Black Death).q: About what share of Europe's people did the plague kill?
wrong: Almost all of them, leaving only a few towns standing across Europe
Your card says about a third.
Bubonic plague (Black Death).exp: About a third of Europe, and many millions in Asia.

How the plague spread.q: Why did trade help spread the plague?
How the plague spread.right: Fleas on rats rode ships and caravans
wrong: Merchants spread it on purpose to weaken their rivals in other cities
How the plague spread.exp: Fleas on rats and other animals traveled on ships and caravans.

How the plague spread.q: How did Mongol conquests relate to the plague?
wrong: They stopped it from spreading by closing the roads between their khanates
How the plague spread.exp: Mongol conquests helped transmit the plague.

Effects of the plague.q: Why did wages rise after the Black Death?
wrong: Rulers ordered higher pay to celebrate the end of the plague in Europe

Effects of the plague.q: How did the plague weaken feudalism?
wrong: Feudal lords grew stronger because they owned more land per person
Your card says it weakened feudalism.
Effects of the plague.exp: Labor shortages raised wages and weakened feudalism.

wrong: His travels to Kublai Khan's court with his father and uncle
Boccaccio.exp: Boccaccio lived through the plague; it inspired the Decameron.

Boccaccio.q: Why is the Decameron useful to historians of the plague?
Boccaccio.right: It comes from someone who lived through it
wrong: It is a scientific study that proved fleas on rats carried the disease

Shared origins.q: Which statement is true of ALL the networks?
Shared origins.right: They built on routes older than 1200
wrong: They were all created by the Mongols after the 1206 kuriltai elected Temujin
Only the Silk Roads were united by the Mongols.
They all traded gold for salt
Shared origins.exp: All built on older routes and grew as states expanded.

Shared origins.q: How did state expansion relate to the networks' growth?
wrong: Networks shrank as states grew, because rulers banned trade with outsiders
Shared origins.exp: The networks grew as states and empires expanded.

Stable states.q: Which pair shows stable states protecting trade?
Stable states.right: Mongols policing roads; Mali protecting trade
wrong: The Black Death and overgrazing, which both disrupted the trade networks
Stable states.exp: Strong states protected merchants and routes.

Stable states.q: What did stable states pay for, according to your card?
wrong: Armies that closed the trade routes to merchants from rival states
Stable states.exp: They funded compasses, lateen sails, saddles and high-yield crops.

Trading cities as \"knots\".q: Which city was a knot of the Indian Ocean network?
wrong: Samarkand, the trading city in present-day Uzbekistan known for artisans
Trading cities as \"knots\".exp: Calicut and Malacca held the Indian Ocean network together.

Trading cities as \"knots\".q: Timbuktu and Gao were knots of which network?
wrong: The Indian Ocean network, which connected East Africa to India and China
Trading cities as \"knots\".exp: Timbuktu and Gao held the trans-Saharan network together.

Centralization.q: How did trade wealth encourage centralization?
Centralization.right: It paid for planning like navies and currency
wrong: It made rulers weaker, since merchants took over all the government jobs
Centralization.exp: Trade wealth funded centralized planning such as Malacca's navy and standard currencies.

Centralization.q: Which example from your cards shows centralization?
wrong: Margery Kempe's book about pilgrimages to Jerusalem, Rome and Spain
Centralization.exp: Malacca's navy is centralized planning funded by trade.

Beyond goods.q: Besides products, what did merchants, diplomats and missionaries exchange?
wrong: Only silver coins, since goods were too heavy to carry on the long routes
Beyond goods.exp: They exchanged ways of life as well as products.

wrong: Gold going north and salt going south across the Sahara Desert
Beyond goods.exp: Ideas, like numerals, moved along with goods.

Silk Roads profile.q: Which network carried mainly luxury goods overland?
wrong: Indian Ocean, which carried goods too heavy to move by land on dhows
Gold and salt across the desert.

Silk Roads profile.q: Which religions spread along the Silk Roads, according to the profile?
wrong: Hinduism and Christianity, carried by merchants traveling on camels
Silk Roads profile.exp: Buddhism, Neo-Confucianism and Islam spread along the Silk Roads.

Indian Ocean profile.q: Why could the Indian Ocean carry goods the Silk Roads couldn't?
Indian Ocean profile.right: Ships moved goods too heavy for land
wrong: The ocean was safer from bandits because the Mongols patrolled it
Ships were faster than camels in every season
Only the ocean had luxury goods
Indian Ocean profile.exp: Indian Ocean trade moved goods too heavy to move by land.

Indian Ocean profile.q: Which tools belong to the Indian Ocean profile?
wrong: Caravanserai, camel saddles and the yam relay system of the Mongols
Indian Ocean profile.exp: Compass, lateen sail, astrolabe and rudder.

Trans-Saharan profile.q: Which feature belongs only to the trans-Saharan profile?
wrong: Monsoon winds, which decided when merchants could set out on their voyages
Trans-Saharan profile.exp: Trans-Saharan: desert, camels, gold for salt.

Trans-Saharan profile.q: Which religion did trans-Saharan trade spread into Sub-Saharan Africa?
wrong: Buddhism, which came along the same routes that carried salt to the south
Trans-Saharan profile.exp: Trans-Saharan trade spread Islam into Sub-Saharan Africa.

Currencies.q: Which currencies appear on your card?
Currencies.right: Cowrie shells, coins and flying cash
wrong: Only gold coins, which every network used in exactly the same way
Each region had its own money.
Currencies.exp: Silk and tin ingots, cowrie shells, metal coins and Chinese flying cash.

Currencies.q: What does the currencies card show about the networks?
Currencies.right: Each region used its own money
wrong: All regions used one shared currency set by the Mongol Great Khan
Currencies.exp: Each region had its own money.

Maritime versus overland.q: As production rose, which trade began to carry more?
wrong: Overland trade, because camels could carry much more than ships could
Maritime versus overland.exp: Maritime trade volume began to exceed overland routes.

Maritime versus overland.q: What did rising maritime trade require?
wrong: More caravanserai and stronger camel saddles for the long desert routes

Labor.q: Which form of labor was common along Indian Ocean and trans-Saharan routes?
wrong: Factory work in large mills, which employed most of the people in each city
Labor.exp: Trade in enslaved people was common along those routes.

Labor.q: Which shows continuity in labor during this period?
Labor.right: Old labor forms continued with more demand
wrong: Free labor replaced all slavery everywhere in the world after 1200
Labor.exp: Free peasants, artisans, debt labor and enslaved people continued; demand grew.

Gender.q: Which is an exception to patriarchy named on your card?
wrong: Chinese scholar-gentry women, who ran the civil service exams for the Yuan
Gender.exp: Exceptions included Mongol women, Southeast Asian marketplace women and European guild women.

Gender.q: Which best describes gender roles in this period?
wrong: Mostly equal, with women holding most of the power in trade cities
Gender.exp: Societies remained patriarchal, with some exceptions.

Centers of learning.q: Which list are all trade cities that became centers of learning?
wrong: Kiev, Baghdad and Kashgar, which were all destroyed by conquerors
Centers of learning.exp: Canton, Samarkand, Timbuktu, Cairo and Venice.

Centers of learning.q: Why did trade cities also become centers of learning?
Centers of learning.right: Wealth and people from many places gathered there
wrong: Rulers banned trade there so that people would have time to study instead
Centers of learning.exp: Trade brought wealth, people and ideas together.

Environmental processes.q: Which costs accompanied the growth of trade?
wrong: Falling populations everywhere and the end of all long-distance trade
Environmental processes.exp: Plague outbreaks and environmental strain accompanied growth.

Environmental processes.q: Which pair connects trade growth to an environmental cost?
wrong: Mongol stability → more forests growing back along the Silk Roads
Environmental processes.exp: Growth strained the land through overgrazing and deforestation.
